pos: n. (George Blaurock, c. 1491–1529, former priest, first adult baptized among the Swiss Brethren, burned at Klausen in the Tyrol)
etymology: German blau Rock, blue coat, a nickname; his family name was Cajacob.
biblical_def: George Blaurock was a Grisons priest who left Rome and joined the circle around Conrad Grebel in Zurich. On the evening of 21 January 1525, after the city council had forbidden their meetings, he asked Grebel to baptize him on his confession of faith, and then baptized the others present — the first believers' baptisms of the Reformation and the birth of the Anabaptist movement. He preached through the Swiss cantons with a force that earned him the name starke Georg, strong George, was beaten, imprisoned and expelled from Zurich, and went to the Tyrol after Grebel and Manz were dead. He was taken there in 1529 and burned. He administered no sword, raised no army and claimed no revelation; he held that baptism follows faith and that the church is a gathered company. Act 8:38 and Act 2:41 are the pattern he returned to. Mat 10:28 is what carried him to Klausen.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an anabaptist as one who holds the doctrine of the baptism of adults, or of the invalidity of infant baptism; and to rebaptize, as to baptize a second time.
webster_full: ANABAP'TIST, n. One who holds the doctrine of the baptism of adults, or of the invalidity of infant baptism, and the necessity of rebaptization in an adult age.
BAP'TIZE, v.t. To administer the sacrament of baptism to; to christen.
CONFES'SION, n. Profession; avowal of a religious faith.
scriptures: Act 8:38
And he commanded the chariot to stand still: and they went down both into the water, both Philip and the eunuch; and he baptized him.
And fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul: but rather fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell.
Rom 6:4
Therefore we are buried with him by baptism into death: that like as Christ was raised up from the dead by the glory of the Father, even so we also should walk in newness of life.
Rev 2:10

Fear none of those things which thou shalt suffer: behold, the devil shall cast some of you into prison, that ye may be tried; and ye shall have tribulation ten days: be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life.
corruption_summary: A priest asked a layman to baptize him in a Zurich kitchen, and the whole Anabaptist movement dates from that evening.
corruption_paragraphs: The January 1525 baptisms are often described as an act of disorder, and from the magistrate's standpoint they were; the council had forbidden the meeting the same day. The question is which authority governs the administration of an ordinance Christ gave to His church. Act 8:38 shows baptism following confession with no civil permission sought, and Rom 6:4 explains it as burial and resurrection with Christ, which is a transaction between a believer and his Lord.

The dictionary distinguishes Blaurock's company sharply from the Münster revolutionaries who came a decade later and are still used to discredit them. Blaurock carried no sword and died unresisting. Mat 10:28 is the text that makes that intelligible: he feared the One who can destroy both soul and body more than the men who could only burn him. Rev 2:10 is the promise he died on.
roots_summary: Greek baptizo (G907), to immerse; sunthapto (G4916), to bury with; stephanos (G4735), a crown.
roots_lines: Greek baptizo (G907) — to dip, to immerse; Acts 8:38.
Greek sunthapto (G4916) — to bury together with; Romans 6:4.
usage: “they went down both into the water” (Act 8:38) — the pattern of January 1525.
“buried with him by baptism into death” (Rom 6:4) — what the ordinance signifies.
“be thou faithful unto death” (Rev 2:10) — Klausen, 1529.

pos: n. (Pilgram Marpeck, c. 1495–1556, Tyrolean mining engineer, civil engineer at Strasbourg and Augsburg, Anabaptist theologian)
etymology: German Pilgram, a pilgrim; Marpeck, a Tyrolean surname.
biblical_def: Pilgram Marpeck was a mining magistrate in the Tyrol who resigned rather than hunt Anabaptists, and spent the rest of his life as an engineer — building a timber flume for Strasbourg and later serving Augsburg's waterworks for two decades — while writing and leading congregations in his spare hours. He is the most balanced mind the Radical Reformation produced. He opposed the spiritualists who dissolved the ordinances into inward experience, insisting on a visible church with real baptism and a real Supper; he opposed the legalism of the stricter brethren, arguing against the readiness to excommunicate over small matters; and he worked out a careful account of the relation of the Testaments, holding the Old as the promise and foundation and the New as the fulfilment, against those who set them at odds. Act 2:42 is the visible church he defended. 2Ti 3:16 is the whole Scripture he refused to divide.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an engineer as one skilled in the principles and practice of engineering; and spiritualism usage follows from spiritual, as pertaining to spirit; not material.
webster_full: ENGINEE'R, n. In the military art, a person skilled in mathematics and mechanics, who forms plans of works for offense or defense.
ORD'INANCE, n. An established rite or ceremony; an appointment; that which is appointed or established by authority.
EXCOMMUNICA'TION, n. The act of ejecting from a church; expulsion from the communion of a church.
scriptures: Act 2:42
And they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers.
All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
For as often as ye eat this bread, and drink this cup, ye do shew the Lord's death till he come.
For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them.
corruption_summary: A waterworks engineer wrote the most balanced Anabaptist theology, against the spiritualists on one side and the rigorists on the other.
corruption_paragraphs: Marpeck's long argument with Caspar Schwenckfeld is the useful part. Schwenckfeld held that the outward ordinances had been suspended until God should restore apostolic order, so that baptism and the Supper could be dispensed with by spiritual men. Marpeck answered that this makes the body of Christ invisible and the Christian life private, and that Act 2:42 and 1Co 11:26 describe a company doing visible things together until He come. The incarnation is his root argument: God works through the material, and a religion embarrassed by water and bread has misunderstood it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Both errors he fought are current. The spiritualist one now appears as churchless Christianity, where ordinances, membership and discipline are optional scaffolding around a private faith. The rigorist one appears wherever a congregation excommunicates over secondary matters. Mat 18:20 gives the gathered two or three Christ's presence, and 2Ti 3:16 gives them the whole Scripture, Old Testament included, to govern it.
roots_summary: Greek koinonia (G2842), fellowship; theopneustos (G2315), God-breathed; kataggello (G2605), to show forth.
roots_lines: Greek klasis (G2800) — a breaking, of bread; Acts 2:42.
Greek kataggello (G2605) — to show forth, to proclaim; 1 Corinthians 11:26.
usage: “in breaking of bread, and in prayers” (Act 2:42) — visible, against the spiritualists.
“All scripture is given by inspiration of God” (2Ti 3:16) — both Testaments, undivided.
“ye do shew the Lord's death till he come” (1Co 11:26) — a bodily ordinance for a bodily people.

pos: n. (Obbe Philips, c. 1500–1568, Frisian barber-surgeon, early Anabaptist elder who ordained Menno Simons and afterwards left the movement)
etymology: Frisian Obbe, a short form of a Germanic name; Philips, patronymic from Philip.
biblical_def: Obbe Philips was a barber-surgeon of Leeuwarden, baptized in 1533 by emissaries of the Münsterite prophet Jan Matthijs, who within a year saw where that movement was going and broke with it entirely. He gathered the peaceable Dutch Anabaptists, ordained his brother Dirk and, in 1537, Menno Simons — so that the whole Mennonite ministry descends from his hands. Then he lost confidence. Having been commissioned by men he now regarded as false prophets, he came to doubt whether his own ordination, and therefore everything he had conferred, was valid at all; about 1540 he withdrew, and years later wrote a Confession that is the most important inside account of the movement's violent wing and the clearest renunciation of it. He died outside any church. Isa 8:20 is the test he eventually applied to the prophets. 1Jn 2:19 is the sober word over his own departure.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a prophet, in the false sense, as one who pretends to foretell; and recantation, as the act of recalling; retraction.
webster_full: PROPH'ET, n. One that foretells future events; a predicter; a foreteller.
RECANTA'TION, n. The act of recalling; retraction; a declaration that contradicts a former one.
ORDINA'TION, n. The act of conferring holy orders; the act of settling a Christian minister over a parish or church.
scriptures: Isa 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.

They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would no doubt have continued with us: but they went out, that they might be made manifest that they were not all of us.
Knowing this first, that no prophecy of the scripture is of any private interpretation.
For the prophecy came not in old time by the will of man: but holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost.
corruption_summary: He ordained Menno Simons and then concluded that his own ordination was worthless, and walked away from everything.
corruption_paragraphs: Obbe's crisis is a warning about how a movement rests its authority. The Münsterite prophets claimed immediate revelation, and Isa 8:20 is the test that would have disqualified them at the outset: if they speak not according to this word, there is no light in them. 2Pe 1:20 and 2Pe 1:21 locate prophecy in holy men moved by the Holy Ghost, delivering what is now written, not in enthusiasts delivering what is now felt.

His withdrawal is the second warning, and runs the other way. Having found his commission tainted, he concluded that no valid ministry existed and left. That reasoning makes the validity of the church depend on an unbroken chain of unimpeachable ordainers, which is the Roman argument in Anabaptist clothing, and Scripture nowhere grounds a church that way. 1Jn 2:19 is quoted here soberly and not as a verdict on his soul, which belongs to God.
roots_lines: Greek phero (G5342) — to bear, to be moved; 2 Peter 1:21.
usage: “if they speak not according to this word” (Isa 8:20) — the test he applied too late.
“no prophecy of the scripture is of any private interpretation” (2Pe 1:20) — against the Münster prophets.
“holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost” (2Pe 1:21) — and not otherwise.

pos: n. (Dirk Philips, 1504–1568, Frisian Anabaptist elder and theologian, colleague of Menno Simons)
etymology: Dutch Dirk, a short form of Diederik, ruler of the people; Philips, patronymic from Philip.
biblical_def: Dirk Philips was a former Franciscan, trained in Latin and Greek, and the most learned of the early Dutch Anabaptists. Baptized by his brother Obbe in 1534, he served as an elder for more than thirty years in Friesland, Danzig and the Prussian Vistula settlements, and his Enchiridion or handbook is the first systematic Anabaptist theology, gathering his writings on the church, the ordinances, the incarnation and discipline. He held with Menno the Melchiorite view of Christ's heavenly flesh, which the dictionary rejects as a departure from Chalcedon, and he was the sterner of the two on the ban, pressing the shunning of excommunicated members even within marriage until Menno himself was pushed into a harsher position than he had held. Act 2:42 and Mat 18 are the texts his ecclesiology is built on. John 1:14 is the text his Christology could not bear: the Word was made flesh.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an enchiridion as a manual; a book to be carried in the hand; and the ban, as excommunication, a public censure by which persons are separated from the communion of the church.
webster_full: ENCHIRID'ION, n. A manual; a book to be carried in the hand.
BAN, n. In the church of Rome and among some Protestant bodies, an ecclesiastical censure; excommunication.
SHUN, v.t. To avoid; to keep clear of; to refuse to meet or to have intercourse with.
scriptures: John 1:14
And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth.
Act 2:42
And they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers.
For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them.

They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would no doubt have continued with us: but they went out, that they might be made manifest that they were not all of us.
corruption_summary: The ablest Dutch Anabaptist theologian held a Christology that cannot be squared with John 1:14, and a discipline that divided households.
corruption_paragraphs: The Melchiorite doctrine of the celestial flesh held that Christ did not take His human nature from Mary but passed through her as water through a pipe, bringing a heavenly body with Him. The motive was to protect His sinlessness; the result denies the incarnation. John 1:14 says the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us, and the writer of Hebrews insists that He took part of the same flesh and blood as the children. A Saviour who did not take our nature has not redeemed it.

The second error compounded the first. Dirk pressed the ban to the point of requiring a believing spouse to withdraw from an excommunicated partner, and Dutch Anabaptism fractured over it for a century. Mat 18 prescribes a discipline that aims at recovery, and 1Jn 2:19 describes departure, not domestic shunning. Act 2:42 is the fellowship such discipline exists to protect, and a discipline that destroys households has stopped protecting it.
roots_summary: Greek sarx (G4561), flesh; skenoo (G4637), to dwell as in a tent; koinonia (G2842), fellowship.
roots_lines: Greek skenoo (G4637) — to pitch a tent, to dwell; John 1:14.
usage: “And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us” (John 1:14) — what the celestial-flesh doctrine denies.
“continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship” (Act 2:42) — what the ban was meant to guard.
“where two or three are gathered together in my name” (Mat 18:20) — a chapter about restoring, not expelling.

pos: n. (Jacob Hutter, c. 1500–1536, Tyrolean hatmaker, organizer of the Hutterite communities in Moravia, burned at Innsbruck)
etymology: German Hutter, a hatmaker, from Hut, a hat; Jacob, from Hebrew Ya'aqob.
biblical_def: Jacob Hutter was a hatmaker from the Puster valley who became an Anabaptist missionary in the Tyrol, where the persecution was fiercest, and organized an escape route carrying refugees north into Moravia, where some nobles tolerated dissenters. Arriving among quarrelling Anabaptist groups at Auspitz in 1533, he reorganized them into a strict community of goods under appointed servants of the word and of temporal needs, and the Hutterite Brethren have maintained that order to the present day. Driven out when the Moravian lords yielded to imperial pressure, he wrote a celebrated letter to the governor of Moravia protesting that his people had nowhere on earth to go. He returned to the Tyrol, was taken at Klausen in 1535, tortured and burned at Innsbruck in February 1536. Act 2:44-45 and Act 4 are the texts the community of goods rests on. Rev 2:10 is the promise over the fire.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines community as a society of people having common rights; common property; and brotherhood, as an association of men for any purpose; a fraternity.
webster_full: COMMU'NITY, n. A society of people, having common rights and privileges, or common interests; common possession or enjoyment.
BROTH'ERHOOD, n. The state or quality of being a brother; an association of men for any purpose, as a society of monks; a fraternity.
FRATERN'ITY, n. The state or quality of a brother; a body of men associated for their common interest or pleasure.
scriptures: Act 2:42
And they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers.
Ecc 4:9
Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour.
Rev 2:10

Fear none of those things which thou shalt suffer: behold, the devil shall cast some of you into prison, that ye may be tried; and ye shall have tribulation ten days: be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life.
(Of whom the world was not worthy:) they wandered in deserts, and in mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth.
corruption_summary: He built a community of goods that has lasted five centuries and was burned at Innsbruck four years after founding it.
corruption_paragraphs: The Hutterite order has outlasted every other sixteenth-century communal experiment, which obliges a fair hearing. Its biblical case rests on the Jerusalem church having all things common, and the honest reading is that Acts describes this without commanding it: the apostolic letters assume believers who own houses, employ servants and are urged to give out of what they have. The Hutterites turn a description into a rule, and the dictionary judges that a step beyond the text rather than a wickedness.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Two things are owed Hutter. His people were genuinely pacific and were slaughtered for it across three centuries, and Heb 11:38 describes them better than any denominational history. And Rev 2:10's promise is the one he died on at Innsbruck: faithful unto death, and a crown of life. Ecc 4:9 remains the plain, modest warrant for common life, that two are better than one.
roots_summary: Greek koinonia (G2842), fellowship; stephanos (G4735), a crown; Hebrew sakar (H7939), reward.
roots_lines: Greek koinonia (G2842) — fellowship, sharing in common; Acts 2:42.
usage: “continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship” (Act 2:42) — the community's charter.
“Two are better than one; because they have a good reward” (Ecc 4:9) — the modest warrant.
“be thou faithful unto death” (Rev 2:10) — Innsbruck, February 1536.

pos: n. (Theodulf, c. 760–821, Visigothic poet, Bishop of Orléans under Charlemagne, author of the hymn Gloria, laus et honor)
biblical_def: Theodulf came from Visigothic Spain to Charlemagne's court, where he was the ablest poet of the circle and, with Alcuin, one of the two intellects behind the Carolingian reform. Made Bishop of Orléans about 798, he wrote capitularies for his clergy requiring that every priest keep a school, teach without charging fees, preach in a language the people understood, and know the Scriptures he read. He produced his own carefully corrected text of the Latin Bible, working from Hebrew and Spanish exemplars. He was the principal author of the Libri Carolini, the Frankish rebuttal of the Second Council of Nicaea's decree on images, which refused both the breaking and the venerating of them. Accused of conspiracy under Louis the Pious, he died in confinement. His Palm Sunday hymn is still sung. Isa 8:20 governed his biblical labour; Psa 119:130 his schools; 1Co 14:40 his liturgical reform.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a capitulary as a body of laws or statutes of a chapter, or of an ecclesiastical council; and an image, as a representation or similitude of any person or thing.
webster_full: CAPIT'ULARY, n. The body of laws or statutes of a chapter, or of an ecclesiastical council; the laws of the Frankish kings.
IM'AGE, n. A representation or similitude of any person or thing, formed of a material substance; as an image wrought out of stone or wood.
HYMN, n. A song or ode in honor of God.
scriptures: Isa 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple.
Let all things be done decently and in order.
All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
corruption_summary: He required every parish priest to keep a free school and corrected the Latin Bible against the Hebrew, in the year 800.
corruption_paragraphs: The Libri Carolini deserve attention because they stake out a position the later church largely lost. Against the iconoclasts, Theodulf denied that images should be destroyed; against Nicaea II, he denied that they should be venerated, holding that a picture is a picture and that worship terminates on God alone. The Frankish position is closer to the Reformed one than anything else in the early medieval West, and it was overridden by Rome.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. What it corrects is the lazy assumption that the medieval church had no interest in Scripture, scholarship or lay education before the Reformation. Theodulf's capitularies require free parish schools, preaching the people can understand, and clergy who know the text. Isa 8:20 and 2Ti 3:16 were not discovered in 1517; they were being acted on, imperfectly, in 800, and the recovery of that fact is itself a Reformation argument.
usage: “To the law and to the testimony” (Isa 8:20) — the corrected Latin text.
“The entrance of thy words giveth light” (Psa 119:130) — a free school in every parish.
“Let all things be done decently and in order” (1Co 14:40) — the capitularies in one line.

pos: n. (Walafrid Strabo, c. 808–849, abbot of Reichenau, poet, exegete and tutor to Charles the Bald)
etymology: Germanic Walahfrid, peace of the pilgrim; Latin strabo, squint-eyed, a nickname.
biblical_def: Walafrid Strabo was a peasant's son given to the abbey of Reichenau on Lake Constance as a boy, taught by Rabanus Maurus at Fulda, made tutor to the young Charles the Bald, and abbot of Reichenau at thirty. He drowned crossing the Loire at forty-one. He wrote the Hortulus, a poem on the twenty-four plants of his monastery garden that is the first garden poem in European literature; a treatise on the origins of liturgical practices; and a great mass of biblical commentary. The medieval Glossa Ordinaria, the standard marginal and interlinear commentary on the Latin Bible for four centuries, was long ascribed to him; modern work has shown it was compiled later at Laon, but his name stayed attached because his gloss-work was part of its material. Act 17:11 is the practice such glosses served. 2Ti 3:16 is why the labour was thought worth four centuries.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a gloss as an interpretation; a comment; explanation or translation; and an abbot, as the superior or governor of an abbey or monastery.
webster_full: GLOSS, n. An interpretation artfully specious; a comment; explanation; remark intended to illustrate a subject.
AB'BOT, n. The superior or governor of an abbey or monastery.
COM'MENTARY, n. A comment; exposition; explanation; illustration of difficult passages in an author.
scriptures: These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple.
Isa 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
corruption_summary: A peasant boy given to an island abbey wrote the first garden poem in Europe and helped gloss its Bible.
corruption_paragraphs: The Glossa Ordinaria is worth understanding whatever its authorship, because it shaped how the West read Scripture until the Reformation. A medieval Bible page carried the sacred text in the centre with patristic comment in the margins and between the lines, so that a reader met Augustine, Jerome and Gregory at the same moment he met the verse. That is a formation, and it had both a strength — no one read alone — and a weakness, that the gloss came to be read as part of the authority.

Isa 8:20 is the standing corrective, sending every comment back to the law and the testimony. The Reformers did not abolish commentary; they relocated it, insisting that the text judges the gloss and never the reverse. 2Ti 3:16 gives inspiration to Scripture alone. Act 17:11 describes readers who search the Scriptures to test even an apostle's preaching, which is the right posture toward every margin ever printed.
roots_summary: Greek anakrino (G350), to examine; theopneustos (G2315), God-breathed; Hebrew torah (H8451), law.
roots_lines: Greek anakrino (G350) — to examine, to sift; Acts 17:11.
usage: “searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so” (Act 17:11) — the posture toward any gloss.
“All scripture is given by inspiration of God” (2Ti 3:16) — the text, not the margin.
“To the law and to the testimony” (Isa 8:20) — where every comment is tried.

pos: n. (Haimo of Auxerre, fl. c. 840–865, monk of Saint-Germain d'Auxerre, biblical commentator)
etymology: Germanic Haimo, from heim, a home; Auxerre, from Roman Autissiodurum.
biblical_def: Haimo of Auxerre was a monk and schoolmaster at Saint-Germain whose commentaries on Isaiah, the Song of Songs, the Pauline epistles and Revelation were copied across Europe for six hundred years, often under other men's names. He is the beginning of the Auxerre school that runs through his pupil Heiric to Remigius. What distinguishes him is a sustained attention to the literal sense and to the argument of a book: where much Carolingian exegesis strings patristic allegories together, Haimo asks what the writer is saying, follows Paul's reasoning as reasoning, and reads Isaiah with an eye to its historical setting before its figures. His commentary on Romans was studied by the medieval schools and read by the Reformers. Act 17:11 names the practice; 2Ti 2:15 the ideal of rightly dividing; Isa 8:20 the standard. Scripture interpreting Scripture is not a sixteenth-century invention, and Haimo is part of the evidence.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines exegesis as explanation; exposition; and literal, as according to the letter; primitive; real; not figurative or metaphorical.
webster_full: EXEGE'SIS, n. Exposition; explanation; interpretation.
LIT'ERAL, a. According to the letter; primitive; real; not figurative or metaphorical.
EXPOSI'TION, n. Explanation; interpretation; a laying open the sense or meaning of an author.
scriptures: These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
Isa 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
Knowing this first, that no prophecy of the scripture is of any private interpretation.
corruption_summary: A ninth-century monk read Paul as an argument rather than a quarry of allegories, and Europe copied him for six hundred years.
corruption_paragraphs: The four-fold sense — literal, allegorical, moral, anagogical — dominated medieval reading, and at its worst it let an interpreter find anything anywhere. Haimo did not reject figurative reading, but he subordinated it to the plain sense and to the writer's argument, which is the method the Reformers would systematize. 2Pe 1:20 forbids private interpretation, and a method that makes every text mean whatever the expositor's ingenuity supplies is private interpretation with extra steps.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The modern form of the medieval vice is the devotional reading that treats a verse as a prompt for the reader's own reflections, and the academic form treats it as a window onto a community's psychology. Act 17:11 and Isa 8:20 both assume a text with a determinate meaning that can be checked. 2Ti 3:16 grounds the whole: the Scripture is God-breathed and therefore says something in particular.
roots_summary: Greek anakrino (G350), to examine; epilusis (G1955), interpretation; Hebrew torah (H8451), law.
roots_lines: Greek anakrino (G350) — to examine, to search; Acts 17:11.
usage: “searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so” (Act 17:11) — the Auxerre method.
“if they speak not according to this word” (Isa 8:20) — the check on any allegory.
“no prophecy of the scripture is of any private interpretation” (2Pe 1:20) — the ground of the plain sense.

pos: n. (Remigius of Auxerre, c. 841–908, monk and schoolmaster at Auxerre, Reims and Paris, commentator and grammarian)
etymology: Latin Remigius, from remex, an oarsman; Auxerre, from Roman Autissiodurum.
biblical_def: Remigius of Auxerre was the pupil of Heiric and the last great master of the Auxerre school, who taught at Reims from about 893 and then at Paris, where his school is one of the roots of the later university. He commented on Genesis, the Psalms and the Pauline epistles, and also on Donatus, Priscian, Martianus Capella and Boethius — that is, he taught grammar and the liberal arts as the servants of Scripture, not as rivals to it. His biblical work carries on Haimo's preference for the plain sense and his habit of following an argument through. Through his pupils the Auxerre tradition passes into the cathedral schools of the eleventh century and so into scholasticism. Psa 119:130 is the aim of all such teaching, light to the simple. 2Ti 2:2 is its transmission. Act 17:11 is what it equips a reader to do.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines grammar as the art of speaking or writing a language with propriety; and liberal arts, as those which depend more on the exertion of the mind than on the labor of the hands.
webster_full: GRAM'MAR, n. The art of speaking or writing a language with propriety or correctness, according to established usage.
LIB'ERAL, a. Liberal arts, as distinguished from mechanical arts, are such as depend more on the exertion of the mind than on the labor of the hands.
SCHOLAS'TIC, a. Pertaining to a scholar, to a school or to schools; as scholastic manners or pride; scholastic learning.
scriptures: The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple.
And the things that thou hast heard of me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also.
These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.

corruption_summary: He taught grammar and Boethius so that his students could read Paul, and his Paris school outlived the empire that funded it.
corruption_paragraphs: The Auxerre arrangement of studies is worth recovering. Remigius commented on pagan grammarians and on Genesis with the same pen, and the order between them was never in doubt: the arts were tools for reading the text. 2Ti 2:2 describes the chain of transmission — Haimo to Heiric to Remigius to the cathedral schools — and the content transmitted was a way of reading, not merely a stock of opinions.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Two failures stand on either side of him. One disparages learning as a threat to simple faith, which leaves the church unable to read its own book in its own languages. The other lets the arts become the subject and Scripture an example, which is what the later schools drifted toward. Psa 119:130 promises light to the simple from the entrance of God's words, and the grammar exists to open the entrance.

“searched the scriptures daily” (Act 17:11) — what a trained reader can do.

pos: n. (Sedulius Scottus, fl. c. 840–860, Irish scholar and poet at Liège, author of De Rectoribus Christianis)
biblical_def: Sedulius Scottus was one of the Irish scholars who crossed to the Continent in the ninth century carrying Greek, and settled at Liège under the bishop's patronage. He wrote commentaries on Matthew and the Pauline epistles, a treatise on Greek grammar, a collection of excerpts, and a great deal of Latin verse, including a famous lament on the deaths of a flock of sheep and a mock-epic on a ram. His De Rectoribus Christianis, on Christian rulers, is the first medieval mirror of princes: it tells a king that his office is a stewardship under God, that he will be judged for his justice to the poor, that he must take counsel and restrain his own appetites, and that a realm prospers or falls by its ruler's righteousness. Pro 11:30 and Psa 127:1 shape its argument. Act 5:29 marks the limit it implies, and Jas 1:27 the measure of a government it proposes.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a ruler as one that governs, whether emperor, king or magistrate; and justice, as the virtue which consists in giving to every one what is his due.
webster_full: RU'LER, n. One that governs, whether emperor, king, pope or governor; any one that exercises supreme power over others.
JUS'TICE, n. The virtue which consists in giving to every one what is his due; practical conformity to the laws and to principles of rectitude.
STEW'ARDSHIP, n. The office of a steward; the management of another's property.
scriptures: A Song of degrees for Solomon. Except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it: except the LORD keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain.
Jas 1:27
Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world.
Act 5:29
Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men.
The fruit of the righteous is a tree of life; and he that winneth souls is wise.
corruption_summary: An Irish poet at Liège told Carolingian kings that their crowns were stewardships and that God would audit them.
corruption_paragraphs: The mirror-of-princes tradition Sedulius began is one of medieval Christianity's real political achievements. Against the pagan and imperial assumption that a ruler's will is law, it insisted that the king is under judgement, that his justice to the poor is the measure of his reign, and that he governs a people God owns. Psa 127:1 makes the point at the level of the realm: unless the LORD build the house and keep the city, the builders and the watchman labour for nothing.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Its live application is double. Rulers who acknowledge no judge above them end in the twentieth century's record, and Act 5:29 is the subject's limit on obedience to them. But the mirror also addresses the governed, since a people who ask of a government only prosperity have accepted the pagan standard. Jas 1:27 measures a society by what happens to its widows and orphans, which is still the right audit.
roots_summary: Hebrew banah (H1129), to build; shamar (H8104), to keep; Greek orphanos (G3737), fatherless.

usage: “except the LORD keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain” (Psa 127:1) — written for kings.
“To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction” (Jas 1:27) — the audit of a reign.
“We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29) — the limit the mirror implies.
